definition: Revel means to enjoy something with unrestrained, exuberant enthusiasm — often used as 'revel in.'
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revel. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revel should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The whole third grade reveled in the surprise snow day, sledding until their mittens froze solid.
To enjoy something is simply to take pleasure in it; to revel in it is to enjoy it loudly, freely, and without holding anything back.
To carouse goes past reveling — boisterous merrymaking stretched into a long, noisy spree.

To bask is to soak quietly in a pleasant glow that comes from outside you — praise, good news, sunshine — the way a cat lies in a warm patch of light. To revel is the loud opposite: enjoyment with every restraint thrown off. Basking is still and content; reveling climbs onto the furniture.

To luxuriate is to sink into comfort or pleasure and stretch it out at length, self-indulgently, like staying in a hot bath after the water cools. To revel is more public and more explosive — unrestrained celebration rather than slow, private indulgence. You luxuriate at leisure; you revel out loud.

A rebellion is an uprising against authority — the same Latin root rebellare that hides inside revel, where the only thing overthrown is restraint.

Closing night ended, the curtain fell, and the cast simply refused to let the evening die.
They dragged the prop couch to the middle of the stage, blasted the show's soundtrack, reenacted every flubbed line at triple speed, and danced in their costumes until the janitor flicked the lights.
After eleven weeks of rehearsal, they had earned the right to revel — and they held nothing back.
The blasting music, wild reenactments, and dancing until lights-out show enjoyment with all restraint thrown off — that unrestrained abandon is what it means to revel.
lively, informal-to-literary; usually 'revel in'

Revel implies open, unrestrained abandon — you revel in a victory or even in chaos — while relish (also in this unit) is quieter and more contained, a savoring appreciation of one particular thing, like relishing the irony or relishing a good meal.

Every autumn, the orchard town of Calder's Mill spends three weeks in silent, aching work, picking apples from dawn until the light gives out.
Then, on the night the last crate is weighed, the town stops holding back.
Workers who barely spoke all month revel in the finish: they drag tables into the street, string lights between the trees, and sing the same six songs until their voices crack.
Visitors are sometimes startled by the noise, mistaking the celebration for a riot of strangers rather than a party of neighbors.
But the old growers say the wildness is the point — after weeks of restraint, the joy has to come out all at once, or the season doesn't feel finished.
